q: A media company stores 400 TB of finished video masters in Amazon S3 Standard. The files are downloaded roughly twice a year, but when they are requested the editing team needs them within minutes. The company wants the lowest possible storage cost that still meets this requirement. Which storage class should the solutions architect recommend?

opts.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
opts.expl: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is designed for archive data that is accessed about once a quarter and still requires millisecond retrieval. It is roughly 68% cheaper than S3 Standard. Deep Archive and Glacier Flexible Retrieval cannot return objects in minutes at their cheapest tiers, and Standard-IA is more expensive than Glacier Instant Retrieval for data touched only twice a year.

opts.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval using Bulk retrieval

q: A company has enabled versioning on a 60 TB S3 bucket. Although the application deletes objects regularly, the monthly S3 bill continues to climb. What is the MOST likely cause and the correct remediation?

opts.text: Noncurrent object versions are being retained indefinitely; add a lifecycle rule with NoncurrentVersionExpiration and ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker actions
opts.expl: In a versioned bucket a DELETE only creates a delete marker, so every previous version keeps billing. Lifecycle rules using NoncurrentVersionExpiration remove old versions and ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker cleans up orphaned delete markers. S3 Storage Lens will confirm how much of the bucket is noncurrent versions.

opts.text: S3 Standard pricing increased; move the bucket to S3 One Zone-IA
Cross-Region Replication is enabled; disable replication on the destination bucket
The bucket is in the wrong Region; migrate it to a cheaper Region

q: A new analytics dataset is being uploaded to Amazon S3. The data science team cannot predict how frequently the objects will be read, and management has explicitly said they do not want to risk paying retrieval fees. Which storage class meets these requirements with the lowest administrative effort?

opts.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
opts.expl: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent, infrequent and archive instant access tiers based on observed access patterns, and charges no retrieval fees for the automatic tiers. It only adds a small per-object monitoring charge, making it the standard answer for unknown or changing access patterns.

opts.text: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
S3 Standard with a 30-day lifecycle transition to S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval

q: A company must retain 5 PB of regulatory records for 10 years. The records will almost certainly never be read, but if an auditor requests them a 48-hour turnaround is acceptable. Which option is the MOST cost-effective?

opts.text: Store the records in S3 Glacier Deep Archive
opts.expl: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost AWS storage, designed for data retained 7-10 years and retrieved rarely, with Standard retrieval in 12 hours and Bulk in 48 hours. It has a 180-day minimum storage duration, which is irrelevant for a 10-year retention requirement.

opts.text: Store the records in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Store the records in S3 One Zone-IA
Store the records on Amazon EBS sc1 volumes attached to a stopped EC2 instance

q: An operations review finds 350 Amazon EBS gp2 volumes provisioned at 1 TiB each purely so that each volume delivers 3,000 IOPS, even though actual capacity used is under 200 GiB per volume. What change will reduce cost the MOST while preserving performance?

opts.text: Migrate the volumes to gp3 and provision 3,000 IOPS independently of capacity, then reduce the allocated size
opts.expl: gp3 decouples IOPS and throughput from capacity: every gp3 volume includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline regardless of size, and gp3 is about 20% cheaper per GB than gp2. This removes the need to over-provision capacity purely to obtain IOPS. io2 is far more expensive and st1 cannot deliver 3,000 IOPS.

opts.text: Migrate the volumes to st1 throughput-optimized HDD
Migrate the volumes to io2 and provision 3,000 IOPS
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on all volumes

q: A company keeps 7 years of monthly EBS snapshots for compliance. The snapshots are never restored except during an annual audit, where a 24-72 hour restore time is acceptable. Which action reduces snapshot storage cost the MOST?

opts.text: Move the old snapshots to the EBS Snapshot Archive tier
opts.expl: EBS Snapshot Archive stores rarely-needed snapshots up to 75% cheaper than standard snapshot storage, with a 90-day minimum retention and a 24-72 hour restore time, which fits an annual audit. Fast Snapshot Restore and cross-Region copies both increase cost.

opts.text: Copy the snapshots to a second Region for redundancy
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the archived snapshots
Convert the snapshots into AMIs

q: A data engineering team writes millions of 20 KB sensor files to Amazon S3 each day. A lifecycle rule transitions them to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, but the bill did not fall as expected. What is the MOST likely explanation?

opts.text: Objects smaller than the 40 KB minimum billable size for Deep Archive are each billed at 40 KB, and each transition incurs a per-object request charge
opts.expl: Archive classes carry a minimum billable object size (40 KB for Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive, 128 KB for IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval) plus a per-object transition request charge. For very small objects these can exceed the storage savings. Aggregating the files into larger objects before archiving solves it.

opts.text: Glacier Deep Archive does not support objects under 1 MB, so the transitions silently failed
Lifecycle transitions only apply to objects uploaded after the rule was created
S3 Glacier Deep Archive is more expensive than S3 Standard in most Regions

q: An Amazon EFS file system holds 45 TB of engineering data, but monitoring shows only about 3 TB is accessed in any given month. The team wants to cut cost without changing the mount points or application code. What should the solutions architect do?

opts.text: Enable EFS lifecycle management to transition files not accessed for 30 days to the EFS Infrequent Access and Archive storage classes
opts.expl: EFS lifecycle management transparently moves files that have not been accessed for a configured period into the IA and Archive storage classes, saving up to about 92% for cold data, while keeping the same file system, mount targets and paths. Files move back transparently on access if that option is enabled.

opts.text: Recreate the file system using EFS One Zone and copy the data across
Change the throughput mode from Elastic to Provisioned
Migrate all of the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive

q: A company runs an on-premises tape backup library and wants to eliminate the cost of tape media, tape drives and offsite vaulting while continuing to use its existing backup software unchanged. Which AWS service should it use?

opts.text: AWS Storage Gateway - Tape Gateway
opts.expl: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library over iSCSI VTL so existing backup applications continue to write 'tapes', while the data is stored in Amazon S3 and can be archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive. This removes physical tape hardware and offsite storage costs with no change to backup software.

opts.text: AWS Storage Gateway - Volume Gateway in stored mode

AWS Backup

q: A research organisation publishes a 300 TB open dataset in Amazon S3. Thousands of external universities download subsets of it, and the data transfer charges have become unsustainable. The organisation wants consumers to bear the cost of their own downloads. What should it configure?

opts.text: Enable Requester Pays on the bucket
opts.expl: With Requester Pays enabled, the requester rather than the bucket owner pays for requests and data transfer out. Requesters must be authenticated AWS principals and must include the request-payer header. This is the standard pattern for large shared or open datasets.

opts.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket

q: An application performs large multipart uploads to Amazon S3, but network interruptions frequently abort them. The storage team notices the bucket's billed size is far larger than the sum of the objects listed in the console. What should be done?

opts.expl: Incomplete multipart uploads leave orphaned parts that are billed indefinitely and do not appear in the object listing. An AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle action deletes parts from uploads that were never completed, typically after 7 days.

q: A solutions architect is designing a lifecycle policy for application log files in Amazon S3. Logs are queried heavily for 30 days, occasionally for the next 11 months, and must then be retained for 6 more years for compliance before deletion. Which TWO configurations are the most cost-effective parts of this policy? (Select 2.)

opts.text: Transition objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access after 30 days
opts.expl: Standard-IA is appropriate once the heavy query period ends at 30 days (it also satisfies the 30-day minimum before an IA transition is allowed). After the occasional-access year, Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest home for the remaining six years of compliance retention. Expiring at 90 days would violate the retention requirement.

opts.text: Transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 365 days
opts.expl: Standard-IA is appropriate once the heavy query period ends at 30 days (it also satisfies the 30-day minimum before an IA transition is allowed). After the occasional-access year, Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest home for the remaining six years of compliance retention. Expiring at 90 days would violate the retention requirement.

opts.text: Transition objects to S3 One Zone-IA after 1 day
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 7 days
Expire objects after 90 days

q: A company is migrating 600 TB of archival data from an on-premises NAS to AWS. The site has a 200 Mbps internet link shared with production traffic, and the migration must complete within one month. Which TWO actions together form the most cost-effective and feasible approach? (Select 2.)

opts.text: Order multiple AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices to transfer the bulk of the data

Provisioning Direct Connect takes weeks to months and is not justified for a one-off migration.

q: A DynamoDB table is configured with 12,000 provisioned RCUs and 8,000 provisioned WCUs, but CloudWatch shows average consumption of roughly 600 RCUs and 400 WCUs with occasional short spikes. What is the MOST cost-effective change?

opts.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode
opts.expl: At roughly 5% utilisation the table is paying for capacity it never uses. On-demand mode charges per request with no capacity planning and costs nothing when idle, which is far cheaper below roughly 15-20% utilisation. Reserved capacity would lock in the waste, and DAX addresses read latency, not over-provisioning.

opts.text: Reduce the provisioned capacity to the observed average and accept throttling during spikes
Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity for the current provisioned levels
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table

q: An e-commerce DynamoDB table has highly predictable, steady traffic that has run at a consistent 4,000 RCUs and 2,000 WCUs for the past 18 months. The company wants to minimise cost and is willing to commit. What should the solutions architect recommend?

opts.text: Use provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling and purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity
opts.expl: For steady, predictable throughput, provisioned capacity is substantially cheaper per request than on-demand, and DynamoDB reserved capacity adds up to roughly 77% savings for a 1- or 3-year commitment. Auto scaling keeps utilisation high. Standard-IA reduces storage cost but raises request cost, and a global table multiplies cost.

opts.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode
Switch the table to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access table class
Create a global table replica to spread the load across Regions

q: An application repeatedly runs a Scan operation with a filter expression on a 900 GB DynamoDB table to find items by a non-key attribute. The read costs are very high. What is the MOST cost-effective fix?

opts.text: Create a global secondary index on the attribute and replace the Scan with a Query
opts.expl: A Scan reads every item in the table and bills for all of it before the filter is applied. A GSI on the queried attribute allows a Query that reads only matching items, typically reducing consumed capacity by orders of magnitude. Project only the attributes needed to keep index storage and write cost low.

opts.text: Increase provisioned read capacity so the Scan completes faster
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache the Scan results
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode

q: A company runs 30 Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instances in a development account. The instances are only used between 09:00 and 18:00 on weekdays but run continuously. Which approach reduces cost the MOST while keeping the databases available during working hours?

opts.text: Schedule automated stop and start of the development instances outside working hours using EventBridge Scheduler and AWS Lambda
opts.expl: Development databases needed roughly 45 of 168 hours per week can be stopped the rest of the time, cutting instance-hour charges by about 73%. RDS instances can be stopped for up to 7 days at a time. Note that storage and backups continue to bill while stopped. Reserved Instances would commit to paying for idle time, and Multi-AZ doubles cost.

opts.text: Purchase 3-year all-upfront Reserved Instances for all development databases
Enable Multi-AZ on all development instances to improve utilisation
Convert all development instances to the db.t4g.micro instance class

q: A solutions architect reviews an Aurora MySQL cluster bill and finds that I/O charges account for about 45% of the total cluster spend. Which change is MOST likely to reduce the overall cost?

opts.text: Switch the cluster to the Aurora I/O-Optimized configuration
opts.expl: Aurora I/O-Optimized removes per-I/O charges in exchange for a higher instance and storage rate, and becomes cheaper when I/O exceeds roughly 25% of the cluster's total spend. Adding replicas increases instance cost, and Backtrack is a recovery feature, not an I/O optimisation.

opts.text: Add two more Aurora Replicas to spread the I/O load

Enable Aurora Backtrack to reduce read I/O

q: An internal reporting application queries an Amazon RDS for MySQL database a few times per hour. Traffic is highly intermittent, with long idle periods overnight and at weekends. Which database configuration is the MOST cost-effective?

opts.text: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 with a low minimum Aurora Capacity Unit setting
opts.expl: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine-grained 0.5 ACU increments within a second and scales down during idle periods, so you pay close to nothing when the workload is quiet. A reserved provisioned instance pays for 24/7 capacity that is mostly idle.

q: A business intelligence team runs a 10-node Amazon Redshift cluster that is only queried during a four-hour window each weekday. The cluster bills 24/7. Which option reduces cost with the least operational change?

opts.text: Pause the cluster outside the query window and resume it before the window begins, or migrate to Amazon Redshift Serverless
opts.expl: Pausing a Redshift cluster stops compute billing while retaining storage, and Redshift Serverless bills per RPU-second with no idle charge. Both suit a workload used only a few hours per day. Concurrency Scaling adds burst capacity but does not remove idle charges.

opts.text: Resize the cluster to 2 nodes and leave it running permanently

q: Analysts query raw CSV files in an Amazon S3 data lake using Amazon Athena. Monthly Athena charges are high because each query scans hundreds of gigabytes. Which change will reduce Athena cost the MOST?

opts.text: Convert the data to Snappy-compressed Apache Parquet and partition it by date
opts.expl: Athena bills about $5 per terabyte scanned. Columnar Parquet with compression lets Athena read only the required columns, and date partitioning lets it skip irrelevant prefixes entirely. Together these commonly reduce bytes scanned, and therefore cost, by over 90%. Storage class changes do not affect scan charges.

opts.text: Increase the Athena workgroup query result cache size
Move the S3 data to S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Load all of the data into Amazon Redshift and query it there

q: A read-heavy application issues the same expensive query to an RDS database thousands of times per minute. The team is considering adding four more read replicas. Which alternative is likely to be more cost-effective while also improving latency?

opts.text: Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster and implement a lazy-loading cache with a TTL
opts.expl: A cache node is typically far cheaper than several full-price read replicas and serves repeated identical queries from memory in sub-millisecond time, removing most of the load from the database. Multi-AZ adds availability but no read capacity, and Performance Insights is a diagnostic tool.

opts.text: Enable Multi-AZ on the primary database instance
Upgrade the primary instance to the next larger instance class
Enable Performance Insights on the database

q: A DynamoDB table stores 8 TB of historical order records. Fewer than 1% of items are read in any month, but the table must remain queryable. Storage dominates the table's cost. Which change reduces cost the MOST?

opts.text: Switch the table to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access table class
opts.expl: The DynamoDB Standard-IA table class reduces storage costs by about 60% in exchange for higher read and write request costs, which is the right trade-off when storage dominates and access is rare. DAX and extra indexes add cost, and PITR adds backup charges.

opts.text: Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
Enable point-in-time recovery
Create a global secondary index on the order date

q: A DynamoDB table stores user session records that remain valid for 24 hours. The table grows continuously and a nightly Lambda function issues millions of DeleteItem calls to purge stale sessions, consuming large amounts of write capacity. What is the MOST cost-effective alternative?

opts.text: Enable DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) on an expiry timestamp attribute
opts.expl: DynamoDB TTL automatically deletes expired items at no additional cost and without consuming write capacity units. It also keeps the table small, reducing storage and scan costs. Issuing explicit DeleteItem calls consumes WCUs for every deletion.

opts.text: Run the cleanup job on a larger Lambda memory setting to finish faster
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode during the cleanup window
Export the table to Amazon S3 each night and recreate it empty

q: A solutions architect is optimising DynamoDB read costs for a high-traffic application. Which TWO changes will directly reduce the read capacity consumed? (Select 2.)

Replacing a Scan, which reads the whole table, with a Query that targets only relevant items dramatically reduces consumed RCUs. Adding indexes increases write cost and storage, and raising provisioned capacity raises cost rather than reducing consumption.
